profile.headline: CS Ph.D. Student @ UMich
profile.summary: I am interested in the design and implementation of programming languages and the verification of numerical programs.

positions.title: Graduate Research Assistant
positions.description: I am working on formally verifying numerical programs under Jean-Baptiste Jeannin.

positions.title: Research Assistant
positions.description: I was working with Professor Justin Hsu and Dr. Ariel Kellison, researching the translation of NumFuzz, a novel language for analyzing numerical programs, to FPCore. My work focused on designing translational semantics that ensured the correctness of program conversions and implementing these semantics in an OCaml tool that allowed users to select different translation modes while preserving the semantics of NumFuzz programs. Additionally, I extended the NumFuzz type system to support operations with varying numeric precisions and improved its OCaml type-checker implementation to incorporate these extensions. Our goal was to enhance the expressiveness of NumFuzz, enabling researchers to apply it in a wider range of settings.

positions.title: Undergradute Research Assistant - Nexus Scholar
positions.description: I worked with Associate Professor Sam Tilsen in the Department of Linguistics on exploratory investigations of subject-verb-object (SVO) sentence production in English. Specifically, we measured how quickly speakers could prepare and produce an SVO sentence when provided with a verb and arguments as visual-orthographic stimuli. We utilized eye-tracking equipment to complement our reaction time measurements. The main focus of our experimental design was to track how the order of appearance of the stimuli on screen affected speakers' reaction time and eye movement. Our goal was to shed light on the effects of non-simultaneity on utterance planning and production, as it could reveal important information about the mechanisms of syntactic organization. As part of my work, I developed a JavaScript tool for running online experiments to measure participants' reaction times to certain images, which were used as norming data for the main study.

positions.title: Research Software Engineer
positions.description: I led the development of a web scraper that retrieved data from the Spotify API, working with a team of two research assistants. I designed the data extraction software to fetch an artist’s albums, release dates, and tracks. The scraper’s backend was implemented using Django, Spotipy, and Pandas, while its data sorting capabilities were built with Python, utilizing data frames to systematically format the scraped information, which was then converted into Excel files for accessibility. I developed the system’s front-end functionality using the Django web framework and deployed the project website on Fly.io to facilitate data analysis for researchers. Additionally, I planned and conducted the migration of the web scraper to Java to improve performance and ensure maintainability. This tool significantly streamlined the data collection process.

positions.title: Undergraduate Research Assistant
positions.description: I analyzed Spanish-language songs that describe the experiences of undocumented immigrants in the United States under the guidance of Assistant Professor Monica Cornejo. As part of this research, I compiled and assembled a list of over 900 songs, delivering weekly reports detailing their content. I quantified the themes of each song in spreadsheets and tracked the total hours contributed by each participant. Additionally, I collaborated with Professor Cornejo and other Spanish speakers to determine the status of songs with unclear content. As part of a larger effort, I helped collect and code raw data corresponding to over 3,000 songs alongside the research team.
